chapter_theme: Impartiality: holding to what is due, whoever is involved, and giving up any gain that requires leaving it. The chapter's central image is the balance, and it treats loss incurred by being fair as no real loss.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: its excellence (111), wealth got with and without it (112-113), how to recognise it (114), gain and loss don't come through bias (115-117), and then it speaks to those in assemblies (118-119) and to merchants (120).

111.reading: That one thing called rightness is good if one can keep to it, part by part, in what is due.
111.nuance: Parimelazhagar says பெறின் conveys how rare this is. The whole verse depends on what பகுதி divides.

positions.position: The parts are enemy, stranger and friend, toward each of whom one keeps the same rule.
positions.quote: பகை, நொதுமல், நட்பு எனும் பகுதிதோறும், தன் முறைமையை விடாது ஒழுகப் பெறின்,

positions.position: The parts are each person's own station, so what is due varies with position.
positions.quote: அவரவர் நிலைமைப்பகுதியோடே அறத்தின் பாற்பட்டு ஒழுகப் பெறுமாயின்,

112.reading: The wealth of a person of rectitude doesn't decay and is a strength to those who come after.
112.nuance: The claim concerns durability, not amount. Parimelazhagar explains that it lasts because it comes together with virtue.

113.reading: Even if it brings nothing but good, let go that very day of gain that comes from leaving what is fair.
113.nuance: The commentators differ on the force of 'even if'. For Parimelazhagar it's only a concession, because such gain can't really bring good. Kalaignar's wording allows that it may, which makes giving it up a costlier demand.

114.reading: Whether people are worthy or unworthy will be seen from what each leaves behind.
114.nuance: எச்சம், what remains, is left unspecified, and the choice has large consequences. Parimelazhagar's claim that the unworthy have no good children is a very confident generalisation, and it isn't in the verse.

positions.position: What remains is good offspring, whose presence or absence is a sure mark.
positions.quote: தக்கார்க்கு எச்சம் உண்டாதலும் தகவிலார்க்கு இல்லையாதலும் ஒரு தலையாகலின்,

positions.position: What remains is the praise or blame left after a person is gone.

115.reading: Loss and increase are not absent from life; not letting the heart bend is the ornament of the worthy.
115.nuance: The verse doesn't explain where loss and gain come from, and Pope's 'not mere accident' assumes one view. The important move is that bias is presented as useless as well as wrong.

positions.position: They are already laid down by past deeds, so bending to get or avoid them achieves nothing.
Rise and fall are simply the nature of the world.

116.reading: If one's heart leaves what is fair and does wrong, let one know: 'I will perish'.
116.nuance: The subject is the heart, so the act is inward. Parimelazhagar draws this out: thinking is the same as doing, and the very thought is an omen to be read. The first-person கெடுவல் யான் makes the warning a sentence one says to oneself.

117.reading: The world won't count as ruin the low state of one who remains in virtue by standing fair.
117.nuance: Parimelazhagar glosses உலகம் as the noble, as commentators often do, and adds that they regard such poverty as wealth. That's a real narrowing, since the actual world may well despise it.

118.reading: To be settled and lean to no side, like the balance that first makes itself level and then weighs, is the ornament of the worthy.
118.nuance: A balance isn't indifferent: it first levels itself, then registers exactly what's put on it. Fairness here is a precise response, not neutrality. Parimelazhagar carries the image into assembly practice, with weighing as hearing both sides and not leaning as stating the result equally to all.

119.reading: Rectitude is speech without bend, provided one surely has no bend within.
119.nuance: Parimelazhagar's corollary is subtle: a correct statement made from a biased mind isn't impartiality. Manakkudavar adds that it excludes clever words which suit both sides.

120.reading: For traders, true trade is caring for others' goods as if they were their own.
120.nuance: Manakkudavar glosses வாணிகம் as profit, so honesty is what actually pays. Parimelazhagar's phrasing, taking no more and giving no less, closely resembles a description of merchants in Pattinappalai, as I recall it. That is my own observation, and it should be checked.

links.note: 112 promises that a fair person's wealth will last, and 117 allows that such a person may fall into low estate. The chapter keeps both. The second stops the first from being a simple reward promise.
Gain got by leaving what is fair should be given up, and in 657 even extreme poverty is better for the worthy than wealth got through blame. The later verse states the cost openly.

On Parimelazhagar's reading, both rest on past deeds, and each draws a response. 379 asks why one grieves at the bad after accepting the good, and 115 asks that one's heart not bend. The first is about feeling and the second about justice.

Parimelazhagar takes 116 to mean that thinking equals doing, and 282 says outright that even thinking of stealing another's goods is wrong. This suggests that the Kural's standard really does reach into thought.

source_issues: Manakkudavar's entry for verse 114 glosses a different text ('ஆரவாரத் தொழிலினானே') and includes an editor's parenthesis about a reading அச்சத்தால். It isn't used as a position here, but the variant deserves checking.
Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 117 repeats his word gloss inside the விளக்கம்.
The Tamil of verse 114 in kg/core reads காணப்ப படும், a typo for காணப் படும். Pope's gloss on verse 119 has a stray space, 'F reedom'.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verse 116.
